rv.q: Hutton thoughtfully explores the gender dynamics of reproductive rights issues by making Val a not wholly unsympathetic middle-woman between the men in power and one of the women impacted by their machinations.

Promethean Theatre Ensemble’s Chicago premiere gives Hutton’s play the opportunity to do exactly what theater should do: make us uncomfortable, make us think, and make us confront issues we might otherwise prefer to avoid.
This production is an undeniably thought-provoking and striking commentary on the times we find ourselves in, and how we plan (and, randomly happen) to be a part of those times.
It's a terrifically tense thriller up to this point. Where it starts to go off the rails is in its last thirty minutes.

The actors do the best they can with the material, but there’s only one moment of genuine emotion, when Nessa (Meghann Tabor on opening night) responds to Val’s hundredth evasion with a scream that’s clearly been building for hours. Overall, it's a gripping production that leaves the audience stunned and talking about the issues.
This taut psychological drama by playwright Arlene Hutton has been set in a near-future America, shaped by post Roe vs. Wade legal and political labyrinths.

cn.t: Critics find this timely dystopian drama about reproductive rights emotionally charged and compelling, though some note it takes an overly deliberate pace. The post-Dobbs premise resonates as both disturbing and darkly humorous.
